questions.question: What is inheritance in Ruby?
questions.title: Inheritance in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a superclass: `class Puppy < Dog; end` — Puppy gets Dog's methods. Ruby has SINGLE inheritance (one parent only). Use it for is-a relationships (Puppy is-a Dog). Override a method by redefining it; call the parent with `super` (super alone passes the same args; super with parens passes none; super(args) passes specific): def bark; super + '!'; end. The ancestor chain: Puppy.ancestors -> [Puppy, Dog, Object, Kernel, BasicObject]. Use `is_a?` to check (puppy.is_a?(Dog) # true). Prefer composition (has-a) over deep inheritance trees; modules (include) add behavior without a parent. A subclass should be substitutable for its parent (Liskov): anywhere a Dog works, a Puppy works. Don't use inheritance for code reuse alone — use it when the subclass truly is a kind of the parent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Ruby has single inheritance (one parent), super calls the parent, and is-a is the right test.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using inheritance for code reuse alone (prefer composition/modules), or forgetting super passes args automatically.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Inheritance = subclass < superclass (Puppy < Dog). Single inheritance. super calls parent. is-a relationship. Prefer composition over deep trees.

sections.title: Inheritance
sections.content:
```ruby
class Dog
  def initialize(name); @name = name; end
  def bark;        "#{@name}: Woof"; end
  def greet(who);   "#{@name} greets #{who}"; end
end

# Inheritance: Puppy IS-A Dog (single parent only in Ruby)
class Puppy < Dog
  def bark
    super + '!'          # super (no parens) passes SAME args -> parent's bark
  end
  def greet(who, style)
    super(who)           # super(args) passes SPECIFIC args
    "#{style}!"
  end
end

p = Puppy.new('Buddy')
p.bark                # 'Buddy: Woof!'  (overridden + super)
p.greet('Ada', 'wag') # 'Ada... wag!'  (super with specific args)
p.is_a?(Dog)         # true  (Puppy is-a Dog)
p.is_a?(Puppy)       # true

# Ancestor chain:
Dog.ancestors        # [Dog, Object, Kernel, BasicObject]
Puppy.ancestors       # [Puppy, Dog, Object, Kernel, BasicObject]

# Single inheritance (one parent only):
# class X < A; end   -- ok
# class X < A; class X < B; end  -- error (can't have two parents)
# Use MODULES to share behavior across unrelated classes:
module Swimmer; def swim; 'swim'; end; end
class Fish;  include Swimmer; end
class Duck;  include Swimmer; end   # both swim, no shared parent

# Prefer COMPOSITION (has-a) over deep trees; use modules for reuse.
# Liskov: a Puppy must work anywhere a Dog works.
```

    super(who)           # super(args) passes SPECIFIC args
    "#{style}!"
  end
end

p = Puppy.new('Buddy')
p.bark                # 'Buddy: Woof!'  (overridden + super)
p.greet('Ada', 'wag') # 'Ada... wag!'  (super with specific args)
p.is_a?(Dog)         # true  (Puppy is-a Dog)
p.is_a?(Puppy)       # true

# Ancestor chain:
Dog.ancestors        # [Dog, Object, Kernel, BasicObject]
Puppy.ancestors       # [Puppy, Dog, Object, Kernel, BasicObject]

# Single inheritance (one parent only):
# class X < A; end   -- ok
# class X < A; class X < B; end  -- error (can't have two parents)
# Use MODULES to share behavior across unrelated classes:
module Swimmer; def swim; 'swim'; end; end
class Fish;  include Swimmer; end
class Duck;  include Swimmer; end   # both swim, no shared parent

# Prefer COMPOSITION (has-a) over deep trees; use modules for reuse.
# Liskov: a Puppy must work anywhere a Dog works.
